intro:
ADHD apps for studying are apps that take over the executive-function work ADHD makes hardest: starting a task, holding focus, capturing a lecture while you listen, and remembering to review. The best ADHD apps for students in 2026 are LessonScriptor for lecture videos, Brain.fm and Forest for focus, Goblin Tools and Tiimo for planning, Chrome Reading Mode for reading, and Anki for flashcards, and most of them have a usable free tier.

No single app covers every study task, so this guide groups 12 apps by the job they do, checks what each free tier really includes as of October 2026, and says plainly where each one falls short, including LessonScriptor, which we build. We are Victoria and Pierre: Victoria studies anthropology online and has ADHD.

sections.heading: What are the best ADHD apps for studying?
sections.content:
The best ADHD apps for studying each remove one specific blocker. ADHD affects working memory, sustained attention and task initiation, so the useful apps fall into five study tasks:

**1. Lecture capture:** listening and writing at the same time splits attention. A live transcript or recording lets you follow the lecture first and process it later.

**2. Focus:** sustained attention to non-preferred tasks is hard. Focus music, gamified timers and site blockers add structure from the outside.

**3. Reading:** long articles and PDFs invite drifting. Reader views, line guides and text-to-speech keep you moving through the text.

**4. Planning:** big assignments trigger paralysis and time blindness. AI task breakdown and visual planners turn them into a first step and a realistic schedule.

**5. Memory:** reviewing on time is one more thing to forget. Spaced-repetition flashcard apps schedule it for you.

The 12 apps below are grouped by these tasks. Every one has a free tier or a free trial, because stacking subscriptions on a student budget doesn't work.

sections.heading: What is the best ADHD app for lecture notes?
sections.content: The best ADHD app for lecture notes is LessonScriptor for video lectures in Chrome, with Otter.ai and Coconote as the options for in-person lectures recorded on a phone. This is the highest-impact category for students. Transcribing lectures or recorded videos eliminates the cognitive load of simultaneous listening and writing—a task that ADHD working memory fundamentally struggles with.

sections.tagline: A live transcript of any lecture video in Chrome
sections.platform: Chrome extension: Moodle, Canvas, Blackboard, Panopto, YouTube, Coursera, Zoom and Meet in the browser
sections.free_tier: Yes: free mode, no account, no monthly cap
sections.price: Free mode $0; AI mode packs from $5 for 5 hours, one-time, credits never expire
sections.best_for: Recorded and live lectures you watch in Chrome
sections.why_it_wins: LessonScriptor shows a live, editable transcript in Chrome's side panel while a lecture plays, so you follow the lecture instead of splitting attention between listening and writing. It works on anything that plays audio in a Chrome tab: Panopto and Canvas recordings, Moodle, YouTube, Coursera, or Zoom and Google Meet in the browser. Free mode uses Chrome's speech recognition through your microphone, so it needs speakers at 80%+ volume and doesn't work with headphones. AI mode captures the tab audio directly, so headphones work, and it is much more accurate on accents and jargon. It has a 30-minute free trial, then one-time packs with no subscription, which removes one more renewal decision. Highlights in five colours, headers and slide screenshots go straight into the transcript, and you export it as .txt or .md.
key_features: Live transcript in the side panel while the video plays
Highlight in 5 colours, bold, headers and bullets, with auto-save
Screenshot the current slide into the transcript
Export as .txt or .md, or copy to clipboard
14 languages; session history saved locally
sections.limitations: Chrome desktop only, no mobile app; free mode needs speakers and doesn't work with headphones; no AI summaries or flashcards (paste the export into ChatGPT or NotebookLM yourself); no speaker labels.

If your lectures are delivered in-person and you can leave a phone mic on your desk, Otter.ai's AI-generated summary and transcript are reliable. However, the 300-minute monthly limit (5 hours) hits hard when you're in heavy lecture weeks, and the subscription model creates decision friction.

sections.heading: What are the best ADHD apps for focus and concentration?
sections.content: The best ADHD apps for focus are Brain.fm for focus music, Forest for a gamified timer, and BlockSite for blocking distracting sites. ADHD brains struggle to sustain attention to non-preferred tasks, especially in quiet environments. The best focus apps work by either providing auditory scaffolding (music designed for attention) or creating environmental friction that makes distraction harder.

sections.tagline: Functional music for focus, with a dedicated ADHD mode
sections.free_tier: Free trial only; no permanent free tier
sections.best_for: Long study sessions for brains that find silence too empty
sections.why_it_wins: Brain.fm is the focus app with the most direct research behind it. In a 2024 study in Communications Biology, Kevin Woods and colleagues at Northeastern University's MIND Lab found that music with fast amplitude modulation sustained attention better for participants with more ADHD symptoms. Brain.fm supplied the music and co-developed the technology, so treat this as promising, industry-linked evidence rather than proof. For ADHD brains that find silence too empty and lyrics too distracting, it is a good middle ground.
key_features: Focus sessions with music built around amplitude modulation
ADHD mode with a stronger neural effect level
Separate sleep and relax modes
No lyrics
sections.limitations: No free tier after the trial; the main study was run with music and technology supplied by the company.

sections.tagline: A focus timer where a virtual tree grows while you study
sections.free_tier: Free Chrome extension; mobile pricing varies by store
sections.price: Optional paid upgrades; check your app store
sections.best_for: Students who need gamification and visible progress
sections.why_it_wins: Forest turns a focus session into a small game: you start a timer, a virtual tree grows, and if you leave to check another app, the tree dies. Loss aversion plus visible progress is a simple dopamine loop, and over a semester your forest becomes a record of the hours you actually studied. The Chrome extension does the same on desktop by blocking the sites you list during a session.
key_features: Focus timer with a growing virtual tree
Allow-list for apps you need while studying
Study sessions with friends
Chrome extension blocks listed sites during a session
sections.limitations: Only works if gamification motivates you; pricing has changed over the years, so check the store before paying.

sections.tagline: Distraction-blocking tool for Chrome and mobile
sections.price: Premium from about $3.99/month on a long plan; $10.99 month-to-month
sections.best_for: Students who need hard-stop blocking of Reddit, Twitter, TikTok during study time
sections.why_it_wins: ADHD executive function is weak at inhibition (impulse control), but environment design is strong. BlockSite lets you hard-block specific sites during certain hours or use a pomodoro mode. Unlike willpower-based solutions, environmental blocking removes the decision entirely. You can't even *see* the site to tempt you.

sections.heading: What are the best ADHD apps for planning and task management?
sections.content: The best ADHD apps for planning are Goblin Tools for breaking tasks down, Todoist for tracking them, Notion as an all-in-one hub, and Tiimo for a visual daily schedule. Task paralysis is one of the most debilitating ADHD symptoms at university. A project due in 2 weeks feels infinite. The best task apps either break tasks into tiny micro-steps (using AI) or create visual progress systems that make incremental progress dopamine-rewarding.

sections.tagline: Small, free AI tools for tasks that feel overwhelming
sections.platform: Web (free); iOS and Android apps (small one-time fee)
sections.free_tier: Website 100% free, no account, no ads
sections.price: Free on the web; mobile apps cost a dollar or two
sections.best_for: Breaking task paralysis on big, vague assignments
sections.why_it_wins: Goblin Tools is a set of single-task AI tools made by developer Bram De Buyser for neurodivergent people. Its best-known tool, Magic ToDo, takes a vague task such as 'write my sociology essay' and breaks it into concrete steps; the spiciness slider sets how small the steps get, down to 'open the document'. That is exactly the step ADHD task paralysis blocks: not doing the work, but working out the first move. The website is free and ad-free, and the paid mobile apps help fund it.
key_features: Magic ToDo: breaks any task into steps, with a spiciness slider for step size
Compiler: turns a brain dump into a task list
Estimator: guesses how long a task will take
Judge and Formalizer: read and adjust the tone of a message
sections.limitations: AI steps sometimes need editing; it breaks tasks down but isn't a calendar or reminder system, so pair it with a planner.

sections.tagline: Simple, flexible task and project management
sections.platform: Web, iOS, Android, Outlook, Gmail, Slack integration
sections.best_for: Students who like structure and recurring reminders
sections.why_it_wins: Todoist is the "sensible" choice: it's simple, cross-platform, and supports recurring tasks (your medication reminder, weekly study schedule). The free tier is genuinely functional. Natural language parsing ("Write essay tomorrow at 2pm") saves friction. However, Todoist doesn't solve task paralysis itself—it just stores your tasks. Use it as the **capture** layer after you've broken tasks down in Goblin Tools.

sections.tagline: Flexible all-in-one workspace for notes, databases, tasks, and projects
sections.free_tier: Yes; free Plus plan with an accredited university email
sections.best_for: Students who need one tool for notes, tasks, deadlines, and resources
sections.why_it_wins: Notion is the Swiss Army knife: it's a note-taker, database, kanban board, calendar, and file repository all in one. ADHD brains often resist tool-switching ("I have to open a second app?"), so Notion's unified interface appeals to that friction. You can build a personalized "ADHD Student Hub" that combines LessonScriptor transcripts, task lists, reading notes, and a semester calendar in one view. The downside: Notion's flexibility is a curse—you can spend hours building the "perfect" system instead of studying. Start with a template (Notion has dozens for students) rather than building from scratch.

sections.tagline: A visual daily planner built for neurodivergent people
sections.free_tier: Yes: basic planner, limited AI chats
sections.best_for: Time blindness: seeing how your day actually fits together
sections.why_it_wins: Tiimo was named Apple's iPhone App of the Year for 2025, and it is designed for people with ADHD and autism. It lays out your day as a colour-coded visual timeline, shows how much time is left on the current activity, and its AI planner can turn a messy list into a schedule. For ADHD time blindness, seeing how much of the afternoon an essay really takes is more useful than another list.

sections.heading: What are the best ADHD apps for memory and flashcards?
sections.content: The best ADHD apps for memory are Anki for rigorous spaced repetition and Quizlet for a friendlier, more varied start. Spaced-repetition apps schedule your reviews for you, which matters because with ADHD, remembering to review is one more thing to forget. Spacing and retrieval practice are among the best-supported study techniques in learning research for every student, and these apps automate both.

sections.platform: Windows, Mac, Linux, web (AnkiWeb), Android (AnkiDroid), iPhone and iPad (AnkiMobile)
sections.price: Free; AnkiMobile for iOS is $24.99 one-time
sections.best_for: Languages, memorising facts, high-stakes exams (MCAT, bar, Step)
sections.why_it_wins: Anki is the standard spaced-repetition app: you make or download flashcards, and its scheduler shows each card just before you would forget it. Since version 23.10 (2023) it uses FSRS, a modern scheduling algorithm, by default. Spacing and retrieval practice are among the best-supported techniques in learning research, and Anki automates the part ADHD makes hardest: remembering when to review. The downside is a steep start, because card creation and deck settings feel clunky. Shared decks for medicine, law and languages save hours.
key_features: FSRS spaced-repetition scheduler, default since 23.10
Create cards or download shared decks from AnkiWeb
Image, audio and cloze cards
Free sync across devices
Open source; works offline
sections.limitations: Steep learning curve; AnkiMobile on iOS is paid; reviews pile up if you skip days.

sections.tagline: Friendly flashcards with several study modes
sections.free_tier: Yes: unlimited sets, limited Learn rounds and practice tests
sections.best_for: Quick review, studying with classmates, language learning
sections.why_it_wins: Quizlet is the gentler way into flashcards. You build a set in minutes or find one a classmate already made, then switch between Flashcards, Learn, Test and Match. The variety helps ADHD students who get bored of one format. The trade-off: the free plan now limits Learn rounds and practice tests, and its review scheduling is less rigorous than Anki's.
key_features: Study modes: Flashcards, Learn, Test and Match
Search sets made by other students
Share sets with classmates
Plus unlocks more Learn rounds and practice tests
sections.limitations: The free plan keeps getting narrower; less control over review timing than Anki.

sections.heading: What is the best ADHD app stack for university students?
sections.content: No single app solves ADHD learning. Instead, use a lightweight four-layer stack: capture, focus, organize, and review. Here's the recommended combination and why it works:

sections.title: The Complete ADHD Student Stack

layers.why: Transcribe any video (lectures, pre-recorded assignments, YouTube tutorials) with zero friction. Your working memory doesn't have to hold both the listening and the writing tasks.
Brain.fm provides neuroscience-backed auditory scaffolding. Forest creates the dopamine loop of visible progress. Together: sustained attention without willpower.
Goblin Tools breaks overwhelming projects into micro-steps (solving paralysis). Todoist tracks and reminds you, so ADHD's weak working memory doesn't have to hold task lists.
layers.effort: 2 min to break down; 30 sec to capture

layers.why: Spaced repetition combats ADHD's weak retention. Anki's algorithm removes the decision of when to review—you just review what the app tells you to. No forgetting when you intended to study.

sections.total_cost: $0/month with LessonScriptor free mode, Forest's Chrome extension, Goblin Tools on the web and Anki on desktop. Brain.fm adds $14.99/month or $99.99/year.
sections.time_setup: 15 minutes total; most tools are browser-based or one-click installs.

sections.heading: How do I choose the right ADHD apps for my study style?
sections.content:
Not every app works for every brain. Match the app to your ADHD profile:

**If you lose the thread during lectures:**
→ Use LessonScriptor to read along with a live transcript, and don't try to write full notes live. Add Brain.fm when you review.

**If you freeze in front of big assignments:**
→ Start every assignment in Goblin Tools. Spend two minutes breaking it down, then put the steps in Todoist or Tiimo.

**If you never know where the day went:**
→ Use Tiimo's visual timeline so time is something you can see, not guess.

**If long readings defeat you:**
→ Open them in Chrome Reading Mode, turn on Read aloud, and add Helperbird's line focus if you lose your place.

**If you don't know what to review:**
→ Use Anki with a shared deck for your course and let the scheduler decide.

**If you need visible rewards:**
→ Pair Forest's growing tree with Quizlet's game-like study modes.

**If you're on a tight budget:**
→ LessonScriptor free mode + Forest's Chrome extension + Goblin Tools on the web + Anki on desktop + Chrome Reading Mode. Total: $0 a month.

sections.heading: Which study methods work best with these ADHD apps?
sections.content: Apps are half the system; the method is the other half. A transcript or a flashcard deck only helps if you have a way to turn it into understanding. Our guide to note-taking methods compares the main approaches and how each works when you start from a transcript rather than a blank page, and our ADHD note-taking guide covers the habits that make any of these apps stick.

faq.heading: ADHD apps for studying: frequently asked questions

questions.question: What are the best ADHD apps for studying?
questions.answer: The best ADHD apps for studying are LessonScriptor for lecture videos, Brain.fm or Forest for focus, Goblin Tools and Tiimo for planning, Chrome Reading Mode or Helperbird for reading, and Anki for flashcards. Most have a usable free tier, so a complete core stack can cost $0 a month.

questions.question: Do I need an app for every study task, or can I start with one?
questions.answer: Start with the task that causes you the most pain. If lectures overwhelm you, start with LessonScriptor. If you procrastinate on assignments, start with Goblin Tools. If you fail exams despite studying, start with Anki. Adding one app at a time is easier than adopting five at once and abandoning all of them.

questions.question: Is LessonScriptor better than Otter.ai for ADHD students?
questions.answer: LessonScriptor is better for video-heavy courses: recorded lectures on Panopto, Canvas or Moodle, YouTube and Coursera, with a free mode that has no monthly cap. Otter.ai is better for in-person lectures recorded on your phone and for live meetings, but its free plan caps each conversation at 30 minutes. Many students use both.

questions.question: Why does spaced repetition matter for ADHD students?
questions.answer: Spaced repetition removes the hardest part of revising with ADHD: deciding what to review and remembering to do it. Anki's scheduler shows each card just before you're likely to forget it, so a short daily session replaces last-minute cramming. Spacing and retrieval practice are among the best-supported study techniques for all learners.

questions.question: Is Goblin Tools really free?
questions.answer: Yes. The Goblin Tools website is free, with no account and no ads. The iOS and Android apps cost a small one-time fee, which helps fund the free site.

questions.question: What if I don't like gamification? Can I skip Forest?
questions.answer: Yes. Forest is optional. If structure works better for you than rewards, use a simple timer and a checklist in Todoist instead. The core stack is LessonScriptor, Goblin Tools and Anki; everything else is optimisation.

questions.question: Do these apps work for professional exams and certifications?
questions.answer: Yes. Medical students use Anki heavily for the MCAT and Step exams, and shared decks exist for most professional certifications. LessonScriptor works on any prep-course video that plays in Chrome, so the same stack carries over.

summary.heading: What's the takeaway on ADHD apps for studying?
summary.content: ADHD is a difference in executive function, working memory and attention regulation, not a lack of intelligence. The right apps take over specific jobs: LessonScriptor captures lecture videos, Goblin Tools and Tiimo get you started and keep time visible, Brain.fm and Forest hold focus, Chrome Reading Mode keeps you on the page, and Anki schedules your reviews. Start with the one app that fixes your biggest pain point, use its free tier for two weeks, and only then add the next.
